name: Dark Orient Blue
lede: Dark Orient Blue is a grayish blue that Ridgway's 1912 dictionary names for "the Orient," a vague geographic gesture that the dictionary never narrows to a place, dye, or textile.

sections.title: A vague place name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 dictionary lists Dark Orient Blue at #436677, plate XXXIV, hue 45″, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 repeats it as "grayish blue" [1]. "Orient" in Ridgway-era English usage meant East or South Asia broadly, but no source we checked ties this swatch to a specific place, textile or dye tradition there, so the connection is undocumented [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[arno-blue|Arno Blue]], 4.6 units away [1]. A little further, at 4.7 units, is [[payne-s-grey|Payne's Grey]] [1]. The Munsell notation is 8.0B 4.1/3.6, and the swatch sits with our [[blue|blue]] family, its gray modifier also pulling it toward [[grey|grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 1.08% of 23,781 paintings, 258 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 109 [2]. That makes it more common than 60% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.4% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 3.2 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a hidden color, in 59% of its 109 appearances, meaning it rarely reads as a dominant tone [2]. Claude Monet painted it most often among the artists in our archive, 4 of his 50 works here, though no painter stands out against the museum baseline [2]. The earliest match dates to 1301, 611 years before Ridgway recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
